one_liner: Vernacular B2B ordering app for small-town kirana stores with next-morning delivery from partner distributors and 7-14 day credit.
sub_sector: B2B kirana restocking with embedded trade credit (lending-led)
ask: INR 2 Cr at INR 12 Cr post-money
business_model: About 4% trade margin from distributors on delivered orders plus a 1.5% fee on credit orders; credit book currently ~INR 85,000.

founders.name: Aarav Deshmukh
founders.background_claimed: 8 years in FMCG distribution and field operations; ran a regional sales team at a large distributor.

founders.name: Pooja Nair
founders.background_claimed: 5 years as a software engineer at a payments company; built the ordering app and credit-scoring rules.

claims.text: Retailer count differs: deck says 38 retailers onboarded; form says 42 retailers onboarded. Both say 22 have ordered more than once.
claims.note: 38 vs 42. Repeat share is therefore 58% (deck) or 52% (form). May be a timing difference, but neither document dates the count.

claims.text: CAC differs: deck gives INR 2,860 blended CAC for October (INR 40,000 field cost / 14 stores); form says CAC is under INR 2,000 per store.
claims.note: The deck's own 12-month target is 'CAC under INR 2,000' (D13), which implies the form figure is a goal, not today's number.

claims.text: How credit is funded differs: deck says the credit pilot is funded from the company's own capital with an NBFC partnership 'in discussion'; form says credit is provided through 'our NBFC partner' and StockSathi takes the first-loss risk.
claims.note: Form also asks the fund for introductions to NBFCs (F18), which is consistent with the deck (no partner signed yet) and inconsistent with the form's credit answer. This is the defining-risk question for a lender.

claims.text: StockSathi is not registered with the RBI as an NBFC.
claims.note: If credit is lent from StockSathi's own balance sheet (D9), whether this falls under the RBI Act s.45-IA registration requirement (W1) is a legal question this research cannot settle; it must be put to the founders.

claims.text: Under RBI's default loss guarantee (DLG) framework, first-loss cover on a digital-lending portfolio is capped at 5% of that portfolio, and an LSP giving DLG must be a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013.
claims.note: The form says StockSathi takes 'the first-loss risk' (F8) without saying how much. Any first-loss arrangement above 5% or outside the permitted forms would not fit the framework. StockSathi is a Pvt. Ltd. company so it can be an LSP in principle.

claims.text: RBI's Digital Lending Directions, 2025 require loans to be disbursed directly to the borrower's account and repayments routed through the regulated entity's account, with no pass-through via LSP accounts.
claims.note: StockSathi's pay-later flow (order now, pay in 7-14 days, D3) settles the distributor first. Who disburses to whom, and whose account collects repayment, is not described in the application.

claims.text: Credit book is about INR 85,000 outstanding across 12 retailers, with no defaults to date; late payments are chased personally by the team.
claims.note: Four months of operation and a tiny book: 'no defaults' is not yet evidence of credit quality. No late-payment / days-past-due data is given.

claims.text: Credit orders are about a third of October GMV (implying roughly INR 1.3 L of October GMV on credit), charged a 1.5% credit fee.
GMV was INR 3.8 L in October; about INR 9 lakh over the last three months; GMV has grown every month since the July launch.
claims.note: Figures are consistent with each other (Oct 3.8 L inside a ~9 L quarter). No monthly series or GMV per store is given.

claims.text: Repeat customers reorder about once a week; 22 stores have ordered more than once.
claims.note: No cohort table (repeat by onboarding month) or churned-store count.

claims.text: Unit economics: about 4% trade margin per order; INR 520 monthly margin per active store; ~5.5-month payback on trade margin; positive contribution once a store has ordered twice.
claims.note: Delivery cost is not shown, so 'margin per store' may be before logistics. Payback uses the INR 2,860 CAC, not the form's sub-2,000 figure.

claims.text: The founders did 60 owner interviews in Karimnagar and Warangal (June-July 2026) before launch; the product is live in Karimnagar only, onboarding via two field agents.
claims.note: Evidence of going to the customer first (R2), but entirely self-reported.

claims.text: Sector mismatch: founder selected 'Consumer tech', but the business is a B2B kirana ordering marketplace with embedded trade credit; 40% of the raise goes to the credit book. Classified here as fintech (lending-led B2B commerce).
claims.note: Relevant to gate G3 (sector label stretch) and to precedent C004: for a lender the deciding question is who owns default risk.

claims.text: Founders: Aarav Deshmukh (CEO) claims 8 years in FMCG distribution and field operations; Pooja Nair (CTO) claims 5 years as a software engineer at a payments company. Neither has prior startup experience; both full-time since April 2026.
Founder LinkedIn links in the form are placeholders (*-example) and the website is a .example domain; no independent footprint for the founders or company was found.
Jumbotail raised USD 120M (Series D, June 2025, led by SC Ventures) and offers kiranas access to credit alongside B2B supply.
claims.note: Contradicts the deck's framing that B2B marketplaces offer only 'Limited' credit on orders (D16); a well-funded player already bundles supply and credit for kiranas.

claims.text: ONDC's DigiDukaan kirana-restocking pilot started in Hyderabad in March 2026 (via ONDC partner Qwipo) and signed up 10,000+ retailers and 35+ brands.
claims.note: Same state as StockSathi; a subsidised open-network alternative for kirana restocking.

claims.text: B2B BNPL providers (e.g. Rupifi) already embed credit into B2B marketplaces in India.
claims.note: Indicates the credit layer can be sourced from specialist lenders; StockSathi's edge must be underwriting/collections in small towns.

claims.text: Application names no specific competitor, only 'Large B2B marketplaces and local wholesale markets'.
Market sizing is top-down: TAM INR 17 lakh Cr from 12M stores x INR 1.2 L monthly purchases; store counts are the founders' own estimates.
Raising INR 2 Cr at INR 12 Cr post-money; three FMCG/logistics angels have invested INR 25 lakh.
Application came via a Fund I portfolio founder. Portfolio company SuperK runs a tech-enabled grocery network for small towns in Andhra Pradesh, which serves the same small-town kirana owners.
claims.note: Possible portfolio overlap (same customer: small-town kirana owners; overlapping job: supply and working capital). Flag for the G1 conflict check; also ask which portfolio founder made the intro.
